# Results — Study 217 (Lipstick Index)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). NBER recession dates are
hardcoded in [`data.py`](../lipstick_index/data.py). Cosmetics basket (EL, ULTA, COTY,
ELF) and SPY monthly total returns fetched via yfinance and cached at
`studies/217-lipstick-index/_cache/cosmetics_monthly.parquet`. As-of **2026-06-16**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| yfinance cosmetics basket (EL, ULTA, COTY, ELF) + SPY, monthly | 1996-01 to 2025-12 | 359 months | `640f285a5058` |
| NBER recession table | 6 recessions, 1980–2020 | 31 recession months in window | hardcoded constant |

Note: the basket is unbalanced. EL (Estee Lauder) is the only ticker available
from 1996; ULTA joins from 2007, COTY from 2013, ELF from 2016. Equal-weight
averaging is done on whichever tickers are available each month. The early period
is essentially EL alone.

## The central test: does the cosmetics basket outperform SPY in recessions?

| Period | n months | Cosm mean ret | SPY mean ret | Rel ret (cosm - SPY) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Recession months | 31 | -1.87% / month | -1.71% / month | **-0.16% / month** |
| Expansion months | 328 | +1.66% / month | +1.16% / month | **+0.50% / month** |

The cosmetics basket actually *underperforms* SPY in recession months by
**-0.16% / month (-1.9% / year)**. In expansion months it outperforms by
+0.50% / month (+6.0% / year). This is the opposite of the Lipstick Index claim.

## Inference

| Test | Statistic | p-value | Conclusion |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| Welch t (rec rel_ret vs exp rel_ret) | **t = -0.357** | **p = 0.724** | Fail to reject null |
| Permutation test (10,000 shuffles) | observed diff = -0.658 pp/month | **perm p = 0.671** | Inside null distribution |

- **The observed t-statistic is negative**: recessions show *lower* relative
  performance, not higher. The Lipstick Index claim is not only statistically
  insignificant — the direction is reversed.
- **Welch t = -0.357** with p = 0.724 is far from the |t| >= 2 threshold. We
  cannot even reject in the direction the folklore claims.
- **Permutation p = 0.671**: the observed difference falls comfortably inside the
  null distribution — 67% of shuffles show a more extreme result by chance.

## The n = 31 problem

Only 31 of 359 months in the sample fall in NBER recessions. The recessions
represented in the cosmetics data window (post-1996) are:

| Recession | Months in window |
|---|--:|
| 1980 recession | 0 (pre-EL IPO) |
| 1981-82 recession | 0 (pre-EL IPO) |
| 1990-91 recession | 0 (pre-EL IPO) |
| Dot-com recession (2001-03 to 2001-11) | 9 |
| Global Financial Crisis (2007-12 to 2009-06) | 19 |
| COVID recession (2020-02 to 2020-04) | 3 |
| **Total** | **31** |

With n = 31 recession months vs 328 expansion months, and monthly volatility
of ~5%, the minimum detectable mean-return difference at |t| = 2 is:
approximately 5% * 2 / sqrt(31) ≈ 1.8% / month. The observed gap of 0.16% /
month is a tenth of the detection threshold.

## Basket composition note

The cosmetics basket changes over time:
- 1996–2006: essentially EL only (Estee Lauder IPO: 1995)
- 2007–2012: EL + ULTA
- 2013–2015: EL + ULTA + COTY
- 2016–2025: EL + ULTA + COTY + ELF

This changing composition introduces a bias: newer, higher-growth names
(ULTA, ELF) pull up expansion returns more than recession returns, potentially
explaining the positive expansion alpha. The pattern is sector-growth, not a
defensive mechanism.

## Could you trade this?

There is no actionable signal here. The implementation would be:
- In NBER recession months: overweight cosmetics vs SPY.
- Problem: NBER recessions are declared with a multi-month lag (the GFC was not
  declared until December 2008, well into the drawdown). Any real-time
  implementation would be delayed by 6-18 months after recession onset.
- Even if on-time: the basket shows negative excess returns vs SPY during
  recessions. This strategy would have hurt, not helped.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Welch t = -0.357 (p = 0.724), perm p = 0.671. The
  cosmetics basket *underperforms* SPY in recession months — the direction is
  opposite to the Lipstick Index claim. No version of this idea clears |t| >= 2.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No tradable signal; real-time recession identification
  is lagged 6-18 months; the basket shows no defensive advantage.
- **BUSTED.** The Lipstick Index is folklore born from a single anecdote (Leonard
  Lauder, 2001), confirmed by no rigorous study. Cosmetics companies have a
  defensive tilt relative to cyclicals — but they do not meaningfully outperform
  the broad market in downturns after controlling for the base rate.
